# Async and concurrency

<!-- Generated by `npm run train` from the sources each rule cites. To change a rule for good, change its source or say so in training/feedback.md; the next training run regenerates this file. -->

- **Implement a single-use, replay, nonce or idempotency check as one atomic add-if-absent on a shared expiring store, never as a read followed by a write (for example `IDistributedCache.GetAsync` then `SetAsync`).** With a get-then-set, two concurrent presentations of the same proof both pass, whether they hit one replica or two that share a store. `IDistributedCache` has no atomic add-if-absent. *Check:* Look for replay, nonce, single-use or idempotency checks that call a get/contains method and then a separate set/add, or that are built on `IDistributedCache`. <sub>Identity ADR-1164; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Consume a single-use record (login transaction, state, one-time code, invitation) with one atomic take that removes and returns it, such as GETDEL. Take it after every check has passed and before its effect runs, never as a get followed by a separate remove.** With a separate get and remove, two concurrent requests can both redeem the record. Taking it before validation would use up the record of a request that is then refused. *Check:* Look for a get then remove on shared state for single-use values, and for takes that happen before validation. <sub>Identity ADR-1164; Identity docs/backend-for-frontend.md; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Update a shared record that concurrent requests or replicas may change with a compare-and-replace on the version you read. Reload and retry a bounded number of times on conflict, and never overwrite it unconditionally. When a single-use token already has a durable row, make the spend atomic through that row's concurrency token instead of tracking single-use state in a second store.** An unconditional write loses concurrent updates, and an unbounded retry loop can spin forever. A second store that tracks single-use state can disagree with the row, while the row's concurrency token already lets at most one spend succeed. *Check:* Look for shared session or state writes that use a plain set without checking the version, conflict retries with no limit, and durable token rows whose single-use state is also kept in a cache or expiring key set. <sub>Identity ADR-1164; Identity ADR-1192; Identity ADR-1290; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Make the update function passed to a read-modify-write operation decide only from its argument, the value as stored, and give it no side effects.** When a save loses a race, the value is read again and the function runs again. A function that uses captured state from an earlier read, or that has side effects, would act on stale data or act more than once. *Check:* In update lambdas, look for captured values read before the call, I/O, notifications, logging of outcomes, or changes to outer state. <sub>Identity ADR-1222</sub>
- **Make a state transition that concurrent callers (requests, background passes, concurrent approvals) can race on check its precondition against the stored value, as an atomic claim that reports whether this call made the change. Only the call that won the claim performs the follow-up effects (notifications, token delivery, audit, logs). It builds them from the record as claimed, not from an earlier read, and it revokes dependent records in the same unit of work. Have the request path and the background pass call one shared helper for the transition.** Otherwise two callers both terminate or approve the same record and notify relying parties twice. Effects built from an earlier read also miss changes made in between, such as a client added to a session that then gets no logout notification. *Check:* Look for transitions that check status on an earlier read, that return void instead of whether they won, effects dispatched without checking the claim result (for example a revoke that returns null or false when the record was already revoked), payloads built from a read made before the claim, and termination logic copied between a request path and a background job. <sub>Identity ADR-1085; Identity ADR-1112; Identity ADR-1222; Identity ADR-1223; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Enforce a count or quota that replicas must agree on with one atomic increment-and-compare on a shared counter before the work runs. Count what is requested, not what later succeeds, and keep deployment-wide rate limits in a shared store, not in per-process limiters such as `System.Threading.RateLimiting`/`AddRateLimiter` partitions.** Reading the count before the work and incrementing it afterwards lets concurrent replicas overshoot the quota, and an in-process limiter admits N times its limit on N replicas. *Check:* Look for counters that are read and then written, increments made only after the work succeeds, and deployment-wide limits built on in-process counters or `AddRateLimiter`. Also look for endpoints that call the counter store directly where the repository registers its limits with a shared limiter. <sub>Identity ADR-1198; Identity ADR-1246; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **In production service code, never let correctness depend on process-local state. State that matters beyond one request, or that another replica must see, goes to the database or a shared-state store, and request handlers never do work that grows with the number of stored records.** Services run as interchangeable, disposable replicas with no sticky sessions. In-process state is lost when a replica is replaced, other replicas can't see it, and replicas apply a change at different moments. *Check:* Look for static or singleton dictionaries, caches, queues or job stores holding state that other requests or replicas depend on, cleanup that diffs against an in-memory copy of earlier configuration, designs that need session affinity, and request handlers that scan every stored record. <sub>Identity ADR-1134; Identity ADR-1059; Identity ADR-1443; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Run work that wholly follows a committed change (cache eviction, change announcements, ending other sessions, clearing counters, audit records, observer notifications) after the commit, on `CancellationToken.None` bounded by its own timeout from the injected `TimeProvider`, never on the request's or host's stopping token. Log and swallow its failures so they never fail the committed write, and put the shared-recorder call inside the recorder so no call site can drop it.** A client that disconnects or a host that stops after the commit would otherwise leave stale caches, live sessions or missing audit records, and nothing emits them again later. Throwing after the commit reports a failure for a write that succeeded, and an unbounded `None` lets a hung store hold the request open. *Check:* After `SaveChangesAsync` or a commit, look for follow-up calls that receive the request token, `HttpContext.RequestAborted` or `stoppingToken`, for `CancellationToken.None` with no timeout, for observer or audit calls made before the commit, and for exceptions that reach the caller. If a publish fails, the announcement that follows it should still run, for example in a `finally`. <sub>Identity ADR-1229; Identity ADR-1230; Identity ADR-1351; Identity ADR-1407; Identity ADR-1412; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity outcomes of #551; Identity outcomes of #620</sub>
- **Once an operation that must not be left half-done has started, such as a remote call that changes state followed by writing back its result, run the rest on `CancellationToken.None` bounded by a configured timeout, not on the caller's token.** If the caller aborts after the remote side has changed state, the local write-back is lost. With rotating refresh tokens, presenting the old token again counts as reuse and revokes the whole token family. *Check:* After a lease or lock is acquired, look for `HttpContext.RequestAborted` or a caller token passed to a state-changing remote call or to the write that persists its result. <sub>Identity review of #420; Identity docs/backend-for-frontend.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Keep the request's cancellation token on work that runs before the commit or that is itself the requested operation, such as ending sessions before a delete, or an idempotent revoke endpoint.** That work isn't post-commit, and a caller whose request fails can simply repeat it. *Check:* Don't report pre-commit steps or idempotent revoke routes for using the request's token. Report them if they wrongly use the bounded post-commit helper. <sub>Identity ADR-1351; Identity csharp.instructions.md</sub>
- **Run a repair or compensating action after a failure on a fresh bounded token of its own, not on the token of the operation that may have timed out.** If the failure came from that token's timeout, the repair throws `OperationCanceledException` immediately and never runs, so the state stays broken. *Check:* In catch blocks that revert or repair state, look for repair calls that reuse the timed-out token or the caller's token instead of a new `CancellationTokenSource` with a timeout. <sub>Identity outcomes of #553</sub>
- **Record a refused credential's failure count on `CancellationToken.None`, and record it before auditing the refusal.** A client that disconnects right after sending a guess must still be counted, even when the audit recorder honours the request's cancellation. *Check:* Look for failure-recording calls that pass the request's token or that run after the audit call. <sub>Identity ADR-1237; Identity ADR-1399</sub>
- **When concurrent callers share one in-flight retrieval (single-flight), run it once on `CancellationToken.None` bounded by its own configured timeout and on its own copy of any disposable input a caller owns, such as certificates. Each caller stops waiting with `WaitAsync(cancellationToken)`.** If the first caller cancels or disposes its input, the shared retrieval must not break for the other callers waiting on it. Without a timeout of its own, the retrieval is unbounded. *Check:* In shared-fetch code (a cached `Task`, a `Lazy<Task>`, a dictionary of in-flight tasks), look for a caller's `CancellationToken` captured in the shared work, a missing timeout, references to caller-owned disposables, and callers that don't await with `.WaitAsync(token)`. *Note:* A per-key gated fetch that runs under the gate holder's token is acceptable when a cancelled fetch only costs the next waiter a refetch. See the rule about not reporting that case. <sub>Identity ADR-1106; Identity ADR-1315; Identity ADR-1400; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity outcomes of #484; Randomness outcomes of #13</sub>
- **In a single-flight fetch wrapped by caches, check the value cache and the remembered-failure cache before joining the in-flight entry, and check them again inside the shared operation. Record the result or failure in the caches before removing the in-flight entry.** A caller paused between the outer check and `GetOrAdd` could otherwise start a duplicate fetch right after another fetch recorded its result and removed itself, so a source that just failed would be fetched again at once. The outer check still lets a cached answer skip the join. *Check:* Look for a `GetOrAdd` with a `Lazy`/`Task` factory guarded only by checks outside the factory, a removal from the in-flight map that comes before the cache write, and an outer check removed in favour of only the inner one. <sub>Identity ADR-1106; Identity ADR-1315; Identity ADR-1400; Identity outcomes of #480</sub>
- **Key a shared in-flight fetch and its remembered failure by everything that changes the outcome, such as the URL plus the timeout and size limits applied, not by the URL alone.** Keyed by the URL alone, a caller with tighter limits makes another caller's fetch fail, and the remembered failure then blocks that caller too. *Check:* Look at the keys passed to the single-flight helper and the failure cache. Report them if they contain only the URI while the timeout or size limit can vary per caller. <sub>Identity ADR-1106</sub>
- **Share a remote fetch through the repository's shared single-flight helper instead of hand-rolling `ConcurrentDictionary`/`Lazy<Task>` bookkeeping for each feature, and have each owner create its own instance rather than resolve a singleton.** A copy of the bookkeeping misses fixes made to the other copies, and a singleton would mix different features' keys in one dictionary. *Check:* Look for new hand-rolled dictionaries of in-flight tasks for remote fetches where a shared helper exists, and for DI registrations of that helper. <sub>Identity ADR-1315</sub>
- **In a background loop or periodic pass, treat an exception as shutdown only when the loop's own stopping token is cancelled. Filter the catch on the token (`catch (Exception e) when (!stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)`), not on the exception type, then log the failure and carry on at the next tick or item.** A timeout from an `HttpClient` or a store surfaces as `TaskCanceledException` while the stopping token is untouched. Under the default `BackgroundServiceExceptionBehavior.StopHost`, one escaped exception ends the worker and stops the whole host. *Check:* Look for `catch (OperationCanceledException)` without a stopping-token filter, filters such as `when (ex is not OperationCanceledException)`, and loops that break or return on any cancellation. <sub>Identity ADR-1223; Identity ADR-1242; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity outcomes of #465</sub>
- **Let an `OperationCanceledException` escape a catch only when it is an `OperationCanceledException` and the caller's own token is cancelled (`when (ex is not OperationCanceledException || !cancellationToken.IsCancellationRequested)`). Treat a cancellation from a callee's own timeout as an ordinary failure, so it is logged, any fallback runs, and the remaining fan-out handlers still run.** Filtering on the type alone lets a timeout skip the fallback and leave stale state cached. Filtering on the token alone lets an ordinary failure reach the publisher once the token is cancelled, so the remaining handlers never get the message. *Check:* Look for catches that rethrow every `OperationCanceledException`, log-and-fallback filters on the exception type, and dispatch loops whose filter tests the token but not the exception type. <sub>Identity ADR-1205; Identity outcomes of #491; Identity outcomes of #617</sub>
- **When a catch handles cancellation during an operation, dispose the resources the operation acquired and rethrow the `OperationCanceledException` without wrapping it.** Wrapping a cancellation in a domain exception turns a shutdown during startup into a reported load failure. *Check:* Look for catch blocks that wrap every exception in a domain exception without excluding `OperationCanceledException`, or that skip cleanup on cancellation. <sub>Identity outcomes of #709</sub>
- **Release a distributed lease or lock with an atomic compare-and-remove against a random owner token that the acquirer stored as the value. Release it in a `finally` as soon as the work ends, on `CancellationToken.None`, and log a failed release as a warning without replacing the work's own result or exception.** An unconditional delete, a version match (a re-added expiring key restarts at version one) or a get-then-delete can release a lease another replica took after expiry. A lease left held makes every waiting replica wait out its expiry, and the lease expires on its own if the release fails. *Check:* Look for lease release by key alone, by version, or by GET followed by DEL. Check that every acquisition has a release in `finally` that passes `CancellationToken.None` and doesn't let a release exception override the primary outcome. <sub>Identity ADR-1291; Identity docs/backend-for-frontend.md</sub>
- **When a background loop acquires a resource such as a session or lease and cancellation can interrupt it before the resource reaches the state that shutdown releases, keep tracking the acquired resource and release it on stop, using a token other than the one that was cancelled.** Otherwise a stop during the follow-up step leaks the resource until it expires, and a restarted node can't reclaim it. *Check:* Look for catch filters that let cancellation escape after an acquire but before the resource is assigned to the field the stop path releases. <sub>coordination outcomes of #23</sub>
- **Run a periodic pass on a multi-replica service under a shared expiring lease so that only one replica runs it, skip the pass when the lease is lost, and keep each item's work idempotent under per-entity optimistic concurrency. Make the lease last less than the timer interval.** Without a lease every replica processes the same items. The timer ticks one interval after the pass started, so a lease as long as the interval is still held at the next tick, and every other pass is skipped. Overlapping writers are kept correct by each entity's concurrency token, not by the lease. *Check:* Look for background passes with no shared lease or with a lease that never expires, compare lease durations with timer periods, and check that each entity changes in its own unit of work with a concurrency token. *Note:* An earlier source keyed the lease by interval window and let it expire at the window's end. The newer source's rule, a lease shorter than the interval, takes precedence. <sub>Identity ADR-1223; Identity ADR-1404</sub>
- **Converge derived state with an idempotent reconciliation pass rather than by replaying events or draining an in-memory queue. The pass reads the persisted store, compares it with a durably recorded last-reconciled input, runs at host start and after every change, and is marked stale in the unit of work that changes its input. Key its lease or dedup key by the input's concurrency token as well as its content, and have a replica that loses the lease retry after a configurable delay.** A queued job or replayed event is lost on restart, while reconciliation can safely run again. Keying only on content would skip a revert to an earlier state. *Check:* Look for derived state updated only by a queued job, an event or a broadcast, passes computed from in-process state, passes that don't run at startup, and lease keys that hash only the content. <sub>Identity ADR-1412; Identity ADR-1443; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Don't rely on a non-durable dispatcher or job queue for work that must eventually happen. Back it with a leased periodic pass, and use the dispatched job only to bring the work forward.** A non-durable dispatcher loses jobs on restart, so the leased pass has to be the durable path. *Check:* Look for required maintenance work, such as rotation, rewrapping or cleanup, that only a dispatched job or a broadcast ever triggers. <sub>Identity ADR-1407</sub>
- **Treat a cross-replica change broadcast as a best-effort, at-most-once, unordered hint. Carry only an identifier of what changed, make the receiver re-read committed state and handle repeated, late, lost or self-delivered messages idempotently, and revalidate on missed messages and on a periodic refresh or bounded entry age.** Messages can be lost, repeated or stale, and the publisher's own replica receives them too. A re-read is always current, and the periodic refresh limits how long a lost message can leave a replica stale. *Check:* Look for message types that carry entity or settings payloads, receivers that apply message contents, handlers that count, toggle or assume they see a message only once, and broadcast-invalidated caches with no missed-message handling and no refresh interval. <sub>Identity ADR-1205; Identity ADR-1407; Identity ADR-1412; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **In production code, keep in-process caches coherent across replicas by applying a change locally first and publishing it only after the write commits. Log a failed publish instead of throwing.** Other replicas otherwise serve stale state, and throwing after the commit reports a failure for a write that succeeded. *Check:* Look for cache updates that are only local, publishes before the commit, and publish exceptions that reach the caller. *Applies to:* `**/*.cs` <sub>Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Have a pub/sub subscriber hand received messages to handlers off the connection's receive loop. Run a missed-messages reconciliation once the subscription takes effect and again whenever the connection is restored, and retry subscribing while the server is unreachable.** A slow handler must not block the receive loop, and messages published before the subscription or during a disconnect never arrive. *Check:* Look for handlers awaited inline in the message callback, no reconciliation after subscribing or reconnecting, and no retry when subscribing fails. <sub>Identity ADR-1205</sub>
- **Hand work to the background or to event handlers as a snapshot (ids, actor, request and trace context) captured when the event is published. Never read `HttpContext`, `IHttpContextAccessor` or request-scoped services from a handler, sink or background item, and run each item in its own `CreateAsyncScope()`.** Handlers and sinks may run after the request has ended, when its context and scoped services are no longer valid. *Check:* Look for handlers or sinks that use `IHttpContextAccessor` or request-scoped state, captured `HttpContext` or scoped services in background work, and events whose data is filled in after publishing. <sub>Identity ADR-1047; Identity ADR-1283; Identity docs/audit-records.md; Identity csharp.instructions.md</sub>
- **Hold an ambient scope that DbContext query filters read, such as the current tenant, in an `AsyncLocal<T>`-backed accessor, not in DI-scoped state or `HttpContext`.** Contexts created by `IDbContextFactory` from the root provider are outside the current DI scope, so they wouldn't see scoped state and their queries would run unscoped. *Check:* Look for a scope that query filters read and that is stored in a scoped service or `HttpContext`, where the context may come from `IDbContextFactory`. <sub>Identity ADR-1018</sub>
- **Don't read `HttpContext` or `IHttpContextAccessor` in interactive Blazor Server components, circuit handlers or per-circuit services. Get the user from the circuit's authentication state or a connection-scoped session.** Microsoft documents `IHttpContextAccessor` as unavailable in interactive components, and the hub's response has already started by the time a component runs. *Check:* Look for `IHttpContextAccessor` injected into, or `HttpContext` used by, Razor components or circuit-scoped services. <sub>Identity ADR-1435</sub>
- **Link any background loop or watch started for a SignalR or other long-lived connection to the connection's `ConnectionAborted` token.** A watch registered as the connection drops is otherwise never cancelled, and the orphaned loop keeps polling for a dead connection. *Check:* Look for per-connection `CancellationTokenSource`s or tasks created in hub filters or `OnConnectedAsync` that only `OnDisconnectedAsync` cancels. <sub>Identity outcomes of #607</sub>
- **Consume a queue of independent jobs with a fixed number of consumer loops over a bounded multi-reader `Channel<T>`, not with `Parallel.ForEachAsync` or a single sequential consumer. Enqueue without blocking or failing the producing request (for example `ChannelWriter.TryWrite`), and log each job that is dropped because the queue is full. Deliver out-of-band notifications, such as back-channel logout, through this kind of dispatcher, not inline in the request.** In `Parallel.ForEachAsync`, one body's exception cancels every running job. A single consumer lets one slow job hold up the rest. An unbounded queue exhausts memory, and a blocking enqueue stalls the request. *Check:* Look for `Parallel.ForEachAsync` over `ReadAllAsync`, unbounded channels, `await writer.WriteAsync` on request paths, enqueue failures that reach the caller, drops that aren't logged, and inline HTTP notifications made during a request. <sub>Identity ADR-1242; Identity ADR-1380; Identity csharp.instructions.md</sub>
- **Make every deferred-job handler idempotent on its dispatch id. Have it throw when a step it depends on fails, so that the dispatcher retries the job, and keep a singleton handler thread-safe.** Dispatch is at least once, and a retry runs every handler of the job again. A swallowed failure loses the retry, and several consumers can run one singleton handler at the same time. *Check:* Look for job side effects that aren't deduplicated, required reads whose failures are caught and ignored, and mutable instance state in singleton handlers without synchronization. <sub>Identity ADR-1242; Identity ADR-1478</sub>
- **Protect shared mutable state against concurrent access, and release subscriptions and disposables so they don't leak. A hosted service that subscribes to change tokens disposes those subscriptions both on stop and in `Dispose`.** Unsynchronized shared state races, and a subscription that is never released keeps firing callbacks and keeps its owner alive after the host stops. *Check:* Look for non-thread-safe collections or fields changed from several threads, shared counts that don't use `Interlocked`, `ChangeToken.OnChange` or `RegisterChangeCallback` results that are never stored and disposed, event handlers that are never unsubscribed, and disposables that are never disposed. <sub>NCodeGroup maintainer: principal-engineer-review; Identity ADR-1433; Identity review of #420</sub>
- **Make a hosted service's `StopAsync` that does work, such as a final flush, run that work once and never throw. Memoize one stop task under a `Lock` so concurrent or repeated stops await it, serialize it with the periodic work, and log, with a defined event id, any data it couldn't save or still held when the stop token expired.** A host can stop a service twice at once. Overlapping stops race on the batch, and the first stop to return lets the host dispose services while the other is still writing. *Check:* Look for `StopAsync` overrides without a run-once guard, without serialization with the timer loop, that can throw, or that drop data silently on timeout. <sub>Identity ADR-1199; Identity ADR-1303; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity review of #420</sub>
- **When a periodic flush fails, keep the failed batch at the head of the queue and retry it before anything else, holding new data in the accumulator until the queue is empty.** Memory stays bounded, and a later batch never commits before an earlier one. *Check:* Look for flush retries that drop failed batches, re-queue them at the tail, or let the queue grow without limit while failures persist. <sub>Identity ADR-1199</sub>
- **Run periodic background work on a `PeriodicTimer` created with the injected `TimeProvider`, with its period bound from validated options, and never let `ExecuteAsync` throw when the host stops.** The registered `TimeProvider` keeps timing testable, periods are validated at startup like other options, and shutdown stays clean. *Check:* Look for `Task.Delay` loops, `System.Threading.Timer`, `new PeriodicTimer(interval)` without the `TimeProvider`, `TimeProvider.System` used directly, hard-coded periods, and an `OperationCanceledException` that escapes on stop. <sub>Identity ADR-1199; Identity ADR-1223</sub>
- **Make services start fast and shut down gracefully: honour the host's stopping token, and let in-flight work finish or hand it off durably. Read and prove start-up dependencies such as keys held in a key management service during the host's startup phase (for example `IHostedLifecycleService.StartingAsync`), not lazily in a synchronous provider or DI factory.** Replicas are replaced routinely. A synchronous resolution that reads from a KMS blocks on I/O, and an unreadable key would only surface at the first login instead of stopping the host. *Check:* Look for background services that ignore the stopping token, long blocking startup work, in-process work lost on shutdown, and KMS reads in keyed-service factories or loading deferred to first use. <sub>Identity ADR-1134; Identity ADR-1479</sub>
- **Serialize per-resource work inside a process with per-key, reference-counted locks that are removed when their last waiter leaves, not with striped locks or one cache-wide lock, whenever the lock may be held across a long wait, a remote lease or I/O. Key nested operations' locks by purpose as well as entity, and bound every wait with a configured timeout that ends in a defined error, releasing the lock on cancellation.** A stripe or global gate held while waiting blocks unrelated keys. An outer operation that takes the same key as an inner one waits on itself, and an unbounded wait or a lock left held blocks every later caller on that key. *Check:* Look for `SemaphoreSlim` arrays or single gates held across network I/O, per-key lock dictionaries that never remove entries, entity-only lock keys taken again by a nested service, waits without a timeout, and lock holders that don't release in a `finally`. <sub>Identity ADR-1291; Identity ADR-1381; Identity review of #420; Randomness outcomes of #12</sub>
- **Publish related cached data, such as a certificate and its issuer chain, as one entry, or only once every part is complete. When clearing a cache whose entries are built from another cache, clear and await the source first.** A reader that sees part of the data, or that rebuilds a derived entry from a stale source between the two clears, builds something broken or stale that may itself be cached. *Check:* Look for two cache writes where the first becomes visible before the second is written, and for invalidation that clears the derived cache first or fires both clears without awaiting them in order. <sub>Identity review of #420; Identity outcomes of #555</sub>
- **Guard a cache load against a concurrent eviction on both paths: don't cache a value, and don't record a failure, from a load that an eviction overtook. Don't zero evicted key material, and zero cached keys only when the owning cache is disposed.** A stale load would otherwise bring back an old key or refuse requests for the whole retry interval, and zeroing on eviction corrupts operations still using the key. *Check:* Compare a load's success and failure paths for the same eviction counter or version check, and look for key caches that zero memory on eviction. <sub>Identity ADR-1235; Identity outcomes of #572</sub>
- **Create a lazily initialized shared client so that a failed creation isn't cached and the next call tries again.** A transient failure must not break every later call for the life of the process. *Check:* Look for `Lazy<T>` with exception caching, or a cached `Task`, that keeps a faulted result. <sub>Identity ADR-1260</sub>
- **Order an outbound call's resilience strategies as total timeout outermost, then retry, then per-attempt timeout, and give every outbound call at least a total timeout. Time a circuit breaker on the monotonic clock (`TimeProvider.GetTimestamp`), and close it only on a success from a call that started after it opened.** The total timeout bounds retries and the body read, and the per-attempt timeout stops a silent provider from using the whole budget. A wall-clock step could hold the breaker open, and an older slow call must not undo a newer failure. *Check:* Look for a different pipeline order, retried calls with no per-attempt timeout, call paths with no total timeout, breaker deadlines based on `UtcNow`, and close logic that doesn't compare the call's start time with the time the breaker opened. <sub>Identity ADR-1336; Identity ADR-1246</sub>
- **Refresh a rotating refresh token single-flight across the whole cluster through a shared lease, not just an in-process lock. Don't rely on an OP reuse grace window or on turning rotation off. Never present a refresh token again after another caller may have used it: when the lease can't be acquired in time, fail with 503 instead of retrying.** Presenting a rotated refresh token twice looks like theft, and the OP revokes the whole token family. Grace windows weaken reuse detection, and RFC 9700 §4.14.2 recommends rotation. *Check:* Look for refresh code without a cluster-wide lease, retry or fallback branches that resend the old token, and configuration that disables rotation or adds a reuse grace window. <sub>Identity docs/backend-for-frontend.md</sub>
- **At logout, first remove the server-side session and delete the cookie on `CancellationToken.None`. Then revoke the refresh token (RFC 7009) on `CancellationToken.None` bounded by a timeout, and log any revocation failure, cancellation included, without failing the logout.** The user asked to leave, so the session must end locally whatever happens at the provider, even if the client disconnects. *Check:* Look for removal or revocation that uses the request's token, revocation done before local removal, and revocation failures that fail the logout. <sub>Identity ADR-1293</sub>
- **Reach a key management service for signing or unwrapping only through asynchronous members that take a `CancellationToken` and return `ValueTask` all the way up through their callers, without synchronous twins. Compute every async signature before writing the JSON with `Utf8JsonWriter`, rather than awaiting in the middle of the writer calls.** A remote key signs over a network call that can wait, fail or be cancelled. - **In production code, never block on async work with `.Result`, `.Wait()` or `.GetAwaiter().GetResult()`, and never write `async void`.** Blocking and `async void` break cancellation and error propagation, and the conventions ban them. *Check:* Search the diff for `.Result`, `.Wait()`, `.GetAwaiter().GetResult()` and `async void`. <sub>Identity convention-audit.instructions.md; Identity ADR-1471</sub>
- **Await a `ValueTask` exactly once. - **Offload work only when it must leave the calling thread, and then use `Task.Run`, never `Task.Factory.StartNew` with an async delegate.** `StartNew` with an async delegate returns a `Task<Task>` that doesn't represent the work, so its exceptions are lost. *Check:* Look for `Task.Factory.StartNew` with async lambdas and for needless `Task.Run` wrapping. *Applies to:* `**/*.cs` <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **When signalling a shared event through a `CancellationTokenSource` that other components register callbacks on, use `CancelAsync` so the callbacks don't run inside the caller, while `IsCancellationRequested` is still set before the call returns.** Watchers must not run inside the caller that detected the event, yet later checks must see it at once. *Check:* Look for `Cancel()` on shared signals called from request or invocation paths. *Note:* Don't ask to replace `Cancel()` where the code relies on callbacks finishing before the next step, unless the repository's conventions require `CancelAsync`. - **In production code, every async method of our own returns `ValueTask`/`ValueTask<T>`, ends in `Async`, and takes a required `CancellationToken` as its last parameter, even when none of its callees accepts one. - **Don't report a trailing `CancellationToken` on our own async method as unused because its callees take no token, and don't suggest dropping it, making it optional (`= default`), suppressing the analyzer rule, or adding `ThrowIfCancellationRequested` just to use it.** The token is part of the method's contract under the repository's conventions, and explicit `CancellationToken.None` at root call sites is intentional. - **In production code, give a method whose work must not be dropped by a caller's abort (post-commit work on its own bounded token, or work a design decision makes uncancellable) no `CancellationToken` parameter, rather than a token it ignores, and record the exemption only with a `[SuppressMessage]` whose `Justification` cites that decision. A justified `[SuppressMessage]` keeps the reason next to the method, while `#pragma` or `.editorconfig` changes hide it or weaken the rule everywhere. *Check:* For an async method without a trailing token, look for a justified suppression. - **Don't ask for a `CancellationToken` parameter on a private shared fetch bounded by its own timeout, on a private helper controlled by a `CancellationTokenSource` it receives, or on fire-and-forget cleanup that must always run to completion.** In each case a caller's token would either have nothing to cancel or would wrongly cancel work that has to finish. *Check:* Before reporting a missing token, check whether the result is shared and has its own timeout source, whether a passed source controls the method, or whether it is cleanup or dispose logic. <sub>Randomness outcomes of #13; coordination outcomes of #22; coordination outcomes of #31</sub>

- **In production code, when an async method needs span work, do it in a synchronous helper.** Spans and ref structs can't live across awaits, and converting to arrays or strings to avoid the restriction adds allocations. *Check:* Look for async methods that copy to arrays or strings only to avoid span restrictions. *Applies to:* `**/*.cs` <sub>Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Don't make a synchronous `Dispose` block on `DisposeAsync` for resources that are only `IAsyncDisposable`, and don't require the two to share one loop body. - **Take a lock scope with a `using var` declaration rather than a `lock` statement or a `using (...) { }` block, unless code after the locked part must run outside the lock. - **Don't report a single-flight cache of `Lazy` tasks as racy when successful entries are never removed and failed ones are removed only by value (`TryRemove(KeyValuePair.Create(key, fetch))`). - **Don't flag an in-memory coalescing set used as a work queue as unbounded when it deduplicates by key, drops nothing, and its documentation explains the bound.** Its size is bounded by the number of distinct keys, not by the request rate. *Check:* Check whether repeated requests for one key coalesce and whether the class summary states the bound. <sub>Identity outcomes of #577</sub>
- **Don't ask for a timeout on give-back or cleanup calls to a coordination provider that run on `CancellationToken.None` by design when the provider bounds each call with its own timeout.** Cleanup runs on `None` so that it still happens after the caller cancels, and the provider's timeout already bounds it. *Check:* Check whether the design records cleanup on `None` and whether the provider's calls have their own timeout. <sub>coordination outcomes of #22</sub>
- **In a GitHub Actions workflow, don't let a job that must finish (such as recording outcomes when a pull request closes) share a concurrency group with a job that sets `cancel-in-progress: true`. - **Cap any computed `setTimeout` delay well below 2^31-1 ms, for example at the regular poll interval.** Browsers treat larger delays as 0, so a timer that re-arms itself spins in a tight loop. *Check:* Look for `setTimeout` delays derived from remote timestamps or lifetimes with no upper bound. <sub>Identity outcomes of #606</sub>
- **Run a long-lived external CLI or child process with a configurable timeout. Kill its process tree on timeout, report the failure, and read its output asynchronously. - **In test projects, test concurrency with gates: a stub awaits a `TaskCompletionSource`, the test asserts state while calls wait, then it releases the gate.
